files.lesson.md: --- order: 19 unit: congruence node: AC9M8SP02 n2 uses: [AC9M8SP02 n1, AC9M7M04 n2, AC9M7M05 n3] assumes: [AC9M8M06 n2] title: Problems with quadrilaterals summary: "Use the properties of parallelograms, rhombuses, rectangles, kites and trapeziums to find unknown angles and lengths, with a reason for each step, and check with the angle sum of 360°." language: maths voice: { name: af_heart, speed: 1.1 } hook: "A gate is braced with a diagonal so it stays a rectangle. A carpenter checks it by measuring both diagonals. Why does that work, and what does it tell her?" connection: parallelogram-linkage app: command: node "$REPO_ROOT/tools/serve.mjs" "$REPO_ROOT/dist/_playground-board" 8325 url: http://127.0.0.1:8325/index.html readySelector: "#gclass" layout: full explainPicture: { ref: quad.yml#explain-pic, caption: "A parallelogram: opposite angles are equal (45° and 45°, 135° and 135°), and neighbouring angles add to 180°." } explainClip: query: { code: "@quad.yml#explain", fresh: 1, id: explain } caption: "Angles in a parallelogram" say: "Opposite angles are equal." clip: - caption: { text: "A parallelogram: A = C and B = D.", say: "In a parallelogram, opposite angles are equal." } - expect: { selector: "#gsum", contains: "A = 45°" } - wait: 800 - caption: { text: "Neighbours add to 180°: 45° + 135°. They are co-interior.", say: "Neighbouring angles add to one hundred and eighty. They are co-interior angles." } - wait: 1800 - caption: { text: "Move A: not a parallelogram, and opposite angles are no longer equal.", say: "Move one corner, and opposite angles are no longer equal." } - click: Move A left - wait: 1600 - click: Move A right - wait: 600 --- Problems with quadrilaterals use their **properties**, with a reason for each step. Start with what you already know: every quadrilateral's angles add to 360°, and co-interior angles between parallel lines add to 180°. ## Predict: one angle ```step stage: predict insight: "Committing to all four angles of a parallelogram from one shows whether they use opposite-equal and co-interior." check: type: predict q: "A parallelogram has one angle of 70°. What are the other three?" options: ["110°, 70°, 110°", "70°, 70°, 70°", "110°, 110°, 70°", "You cannot tell"] actual: "110°, 70° and 110°. The opposite angle is equal (70°), and each neighbour is 180° − 70° = 110°." ``` Picture the parallelogram, with its 70° angle in one corner. ## Run: make a parallelogram ```step stage: run insight: "Making parallelograms on the board shows opposite angles equal and neighbours adding to 180° every time." try: { playground: board, starter: "quad.yml#run", height: 640 } check: { type: board, text: "Drag the corners to make a parallelogram that is not a rectangle. Check the angles: were you right?", when: "z = 4", explain: "Opposite angles are equal and each pair of neighbours adds to 180°, whatever the parallelogram." } ``` Here are the properties to use: | Shape | Angles | Diagonals | |---|---|---| | any quadrilateral | add to 360° | | | parallelogram | opposite angles equal; neighbours add to 180° | bisect each other | | rhombus | as a parallelogram | bisect each other at 90° | | rectangle | four right angles | equal, and bisect each other | | kite | the angles between the unequal sides are equal | cross at 90° | | isosceles trapezium | base angles equal (in pairs) | equal | Neighbouring angles of a parallelogram add to 180° because they are **co-interior** angles between parallel sides. ## Investigate: find the angles ```step stage: investigate insight: "Use co-interior angles for neighbours and equality for opposites, with reasons; opposite angles adding to 180° is the slip (Jo); a kite's equal angles come from congruent triangles." tasks: - check: type: number q: "In parallelogram PQRS, angle P = 65°. What is angle Q, in degrees?" answer: 115 tolerance: 0 feedback: - ["65", "Q is next to P, not opposite. Neighbouring angles add to 180°."] explain: "P and Q are co-interior angles between the parallel sides PS and QR: 180 − 65 = 115°." - check: type: bug code: "working.txt#jo" text: "Jo works out the angles of a parallelogram. Click the line where she goes wrong." answer: 2 fault: logic misconception: opp-angles-supplementary explain: "Line 2: opposite angles are equal, so C = 65°. Neighbouring angles add to 180°. Then D = 115°." - check: type: question q: "Kite ABCD has AB = AD and CB = CD, and angle B = 100°. Which other angle must be 100°, and why?" options: ["Angle D: triangles ABC and ADC are congruent (SSS)", "Angle A: it is opposite", "Angle C: it is next to B", "None of them"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "A is next to B, not opposite it; D is opposite B.", "C is between CB and CD, next to B.", "The congruent triangles give one equal pair."] explain: "AB = AD, CB = CD and AC is shared, so the triangles are congruent and angle B = angle D." ``` ### Neighbours Here is the routine. ```worked \angle K = 72^\circ \text{ in parallelogram } KLMN :: What is given? \angle K + \angle L = 180^\circ :: Co-interior angles: KN is parallel to LM. \angle L = 180^\circ - 72^\circ = 108^\circ :: Work it out. \angle M = 72^\circ,\ \angle N = 108^\circ :: Opposite angles are equal. Check: they add to 360°. ``` ### Find the mistake Read Jo's working. Which angle is opposite A? ### A kite ## Modify: other shapes ```step stage: modify insight: "The same reasoning on a rhombus, a rectangle's diagonals, a kite and an isosceles trapezium." tasks: - check: type: number q: "A rhombus has an angle of 70°. What is the size of its larger angles, in degrees?" answer: 110 tolerance: 0 explain: "A rhombus is a parallelogram: neighbouring angles add to 180°, so 180 − 70 = 110°." - check: type: number q: "Rectangle ABCD has diagonals that cross at M. AC = 10 cm. How long is BM, in cm?" answer: 5 tolerance: 0 feedback: - ["10", "BM is half of BD."] explain: "The diagonals are equal (BD = 10) and cut each other in half, so BM = 5 cm." - check: type: number q: "Kite ABCD has AB = AD and CB = CD. Angle A = 70° and angle C = 90°. What is angle B, in degrees?" answer: 100 tolerance: 0 feedback: - ["200", "200° is B and D together."] explain: "Angles B and D are equal (congruent triangles). 360 − 70 − 90 = 200, so each is 100°." - check: type: number q: "An isosceles trapezium has two base angles of 70°. What is each of the other two angles, in degrees?" answer: 110 tolerance: 0 explain: "Each top angle is co-interior with a base angle: 180 − 70 = 110°. Check: 70 + 70 + 110 + 110 = 360." ``` ### Rhombus ### Rectangle diagonals ### Kite ### Isosceles trapezium ## Practise: quadrilateral problems ```step stage: practise insight: "Angles with algebra, diagonals and Pythagoras, mixed; opposite angles as supplementary is the planted slip again; similar shapes review." tasks: - check: type: number q: "Two neighbouring angles of a parallelogram are x° and 2x°. What is x?" answer: 60 tolerance: 0 feedback: - ["120", "That is 2x. Solve x + 2x = 180."] explain: "x + 2x = 180, so 3x = 180 and x = 60. The angles are 60° and 120°." - check: type: number q: "A rhombus has diagonals of 6 cm and 8 cm. How long is each side, in cm?" answer: 5 tolerance: 0 explain: "The diagonals cut each other in half at 90°, making right-angled triangles with legs 3 and 4: the side is 5 cm." - check: type: number q: "In parallelogram ABCD, angle A = 52°. What is angle C, in degrees?" answer: 52 tolerance: 0 feedback: - ["128", "C is opposite A, not next to it. Opposite angles are equal."] explain: "Opposite angles of a parallelogram are equal: 52°." - check: type: number q: "Review: a 2 cm by 3 cm rectangle is enlarged with scale factor 4. What is the longer side now, in cm?" answer: 12 tolerance: 0 explain: "3 × 4 = 12 cm." ``` ### Angles with x ### Rhombus sides ### Opposite angles ### Review: similar shapes ## Make: a right-angled kite ```step stage: make insight: "Building a kite with a given angle, then solving for the others, joins the board, the properties and the angle sum." try: { playground: board, starter: "quad.yml#make", height: 640 } hint: ["A kite has AB = AD and CB = CD.", "Put B and D level, the same distance either side of A, so that angle A is 90°.", "Try A at 5,1, B at 7,3 and D at 3,3, then move C up the middle."] check: { type: board, text: "Make a kite (not a square) with a right angle at A, where AB = AD.", when: "z = 6 and a = 90", explain: "Such as corners 5,1; 7,3; 5,7; 3,3. Angles B and D are equal (congruent triangles), and all four add to 360°." } ``` Then read angle C on the board and work out angles B and D, with a reason for each. The board rounds each angle to a whole degree, so its B and D can differ by 1°: your answer can be a half. ## Make: a linkage tray, on paper ```step stage: make insight: "A swinging toolbox tray is a parallelogram: neighbouring angles are co-interior, so they add to 180°, and the four angles add to 360° as a check." hint: ["Is angle B next to A or opposite it?", "Neighbouring angles of a parallelogram add to 180°."] check: type: reasoning paper: true q: "A toolbox tray swings on two equal arms, so its hinge points A, B, C and D make a parallelogram. With the tray open, angle A is 64°. Find angle B, and check the four angles add to 360°." steps: - ["$A$ and $B$ are neighbours, between the parallel sides $AD$ and $BC$", "they are co-interior angles"] - ["$A + B = 180^\\circ$", "co-interior angles between parallel sides add to $180^\\circ$"] - ["$B = 180^\\circ - 64^\\circ = 116^\\circ$", "take $A$ away from $180^\\circ$"] - ["$C = 64^\\circ$ and $D = 116^\\circ$, and $64 + 116 + 64 + 116 = 360$", "opposite angles are equal; check with the angle sum of $360^\\circ$"] picks: - step: 2 q: "Why can you find B from A like this?" options: - "A and B are neighbours between parallel sides, so they add to 180°" - "A and B are opposite, so they are equal" - "A and B must add to 360°, like all four angles" answer: 0 feedback: [null, "Opposite angles are equal, but B is next to A, not opposite it.", "360° is for all four angles together. Two neighbours add to 180°."] answer: "116" tolerance: 0 feedback: - ["64", "That is angle A. B is next to it, so B and A add to 180°."] - ["296", "That is 360° − 64°, all three other angles together. Take A from 180° for its neighbour."] criteria: - "I wrote that A and B are co-interior, so they add to 180°." - "I found C and D as well." - "I checked that all four angles add to 360°." explain: "A and B are neighbours between parallel sides, so B = 180° − 64° = 116°. Then C = 64° and D = 116°, and the four add to 360°." ``` Do this one in your book, not on the screen. The angle is made up for the task; real trays have arms that stop at a set angle. Write the reason for each line, check with 360°, and type angle B. **Also used in** - **Desk lamps and barriers.** Lamp arms and car-park barriers use the same parallelogram linkage, so the lamp head or the barrier arm keeps its direction as it moves. - **Garden beds.** Setting out a parallelogram-shaped bed means knowing which sides and angles must match. - **Frames.** A carpenter measures a frame's two diagonals: equal ones show a parallelogram frame is a rectangle. ```teacher summary: Students use the angle and diagonal properties of quadrilaterals to find unknown angles and lengths, with reasons (AC9M8SP02, node 2). time: 40 timing: Predict and Run 8 min · Investigate 10 min · Modify 10 min · Practise and Make 12 min goals: - I can find unknown angles in parallelograms, rhombuses, kites and trapeziums. - I can use diagonal properties to find lengths. - I can give a reason for each step. struggle: Telling opposite from neighbouring angles. Ask students to trace the parallel sides with a finger before they decide which rule applies. before: > Do the Run board yourself first. Students need the quadrilateral family, co-interior angles and the angle sum of a quadrilateral (Year 7), and the proofs from the last lesson. The one idea: each property is a rule with a reason, so a problem is a chain of rules. The common mistake is saying opposite angles of a parallelogram add to 180° (Jo's mistake); neighbouring angles do. Reasons students should use: co-interior angles, opposite angles of a parallelogram, angle sum of a quadrilateral (360°), properties of the diagonals, congruent triangles. Wider: the carpenter's check in the hook (equal diagonals mean a parallelogram frame is a rectangle). running: - "Predict: ask which angle is opposite the 70° one." - "Run: ask what stays the same as the parallelogram changes." - "Investigate: ask Jo which pairs are co-interior." - "Modify: ask for a check using 360°." - "Make: ask which angles of the kite must be equal, and why." - "Paper: the linkage task is worked in books; the page marks angle B (116) and the reason for using 180°. Books out, then look at the page for the 360° check, not the screen." stuck: - see: A student subtracts from 180 for the opposite angle. ask: Are those two angles between the same pair of parallel sides? fix: Opposite angles are equal; neighbours add to 180°. - see: A student uses the whole diagonal for half. ask: Where do the diagonals cross? fix: "They cut each other in half: each part is half the diagonal." - see: A student gives answers with no reasons. ask: Which property did you use? fix: Write the reason after each line, such as 'co-interior angles'. stretch: "Prove the carpenter's check: a parallelogram with equal diagonals is a rectangle." support: The properties table from the lesson, printed with a column for 'reason words'. leads: > This completes AC9M8SP02. Where it leads: congruence algorithms (next lesson), and circle geometry and trigonometry in Years 9 and 10. exit: q: In parallelogram ABCD, angle B = 3 × angle A. Find all four angles. a: A + 3A = 180, so A = 45°. B = 135°, C = 45°, D = 135°. explain: > Use the **properties**, with a reason for each step. A **parallelogram**'s opposite angles are equal and its neighbouring (co-interior) angles add to 180°. A **kite** has one pair of equal opposite angles. A **rectangle**'s diagonals are equal and cut each other in half; a **rhombus**'s cut each other in half at 90°. Every quadrilateral's angles add to 360°: use it to check. ```

files.working.txt:
# Jo's working for the "find the mistake" task. Plain text: students click the wrong line, nothing runs.

# region: jo
ABCD is a parallelogram with angle A = 65°.
Opposite angles add to 180°, so angle C = 180° − 65° = 115°.
Angles A and B are co-interior, so angle B = 180° − 65° = 115°.
So the angles are A = 65°, B = 115°, C = 115° and D = 65°.
# endregion
